title: ALMA finds a fully heavy version of methanol around a young star
freshness: Belloche et al. first posted their accepted Astronomy & Astrophysics manuscript on October 5, 2026; ALMA released the result on October 7, 2026. Preferred 15-day window.
excerpt: ALMA has detected CD₃OD, a rare form of methanol in which every hydrogen atom is replaced by heavier deuterium, around a young star about 1,000 light-years away. Its chemical fingerprint challenges models of how molecules form in the cold clouds that give birth to stars.
whyItMatters: Different forms of methanol preserve clues about cold chemistry before and during star formation. The first secure interstellar detection of fully deuterated methanol offers a new test of chemical models and how organic material may be inherited by forming planetary systems.

exploreFurther.label: Read Belloche et al.'s accepted manuscript

whatToExploreNext: Do other protostars show the same pattern of heavy-methanol enrichment, or does it depend on the conditions in each parent cloud?

sources.label: Belloche et al., COMPASS VII, accepted Astronomy & Astrophysics manuscript

body:
## An alcohol with every hydrogen replaced

Around a young star in the Perseus molecular cloud, astronomers have identified a version of methanol that had never been securely detected in interstellar space. Its chemical formula is CD₃OD. Ordinary methanol is CH₃OH, but in this rare form, all four hydrogen atoms have been replaced by deuterium, a heavier variety of hydrogen with an extra neutron.

The signal came from material surrounding IRAS 4A2, one member of a young stellar pair about 1,000 light-years away. It was found in observations from ALMA, an array of radio dishes in Chile. The result is part of COMPASS, a survey designed to compare the chemistry of eleven low-mass protostellar systems. A protostar is a star still gathering material and developing toward its stable, hydrogen-burning life.

## How a molecule leaves a fingerprint

Astronomers did not collect a sample of the gas. They identified the molecule from the particular frequencies at which it emits radiation. Molecules rotate in quantized ways, and each arrangement of atoms produces a characteristic set of spectral lines. Replacing hydrogen with deuterium changes the molecule's mass and shifts those lines.

The research team compared ALMA's observed spectrum with laboratory-based predictions for methanol and its isotopic variants. They modeled the contributions of many other molecules, because the region is crowded with overlapping signals. The resulting match supports the first robust identification of fully deuterated methanol in the interstellar medium. Earlier searches had produced hints, but not a secure identification.

This is not a discovery of alcohol floating in a drinkable cloud. Methanol is toxic, and the word *organic* describes its carbon-based chemistry, not a biological origin. The value of this detection lies in what the atom substitutions can reveal about conditions long before a star finishes forming.

## A record of cold chemistry

Methanol can form on the icy surfaces of tiny dust grains inside very cold molecular clouds. In such conditions, chemical reactions can make deuterium unusually likely to enter newly formed molecules, even though ordinary hydrogen is far more common. Later, as a protostar warms its surroundings, molecules trapped in ice can enter the gas and become visible to radio telescopes.

By measuring several methanol variants, researchers can compare how frequently one, two, three, or four hydrogen atoms were replaced. Those patterns act as clues to the chemical history of the cloud. In IRAS 4A2, the inferred enrichment rises for more heavily substituted versions. Existing chemical models of cold cores and young stellar environments do not reproduce the full pattern quantitatively, and the detection of CD₃OD makes the mismatch harder to ignore.

There is an important qualification. The team inferred molecular abundances by modeling how radiation passes through the gas under a local thermodynamic equilibrium assumption. They suspect their estimate for ordinary methanol may be too low, perhaps because the emitting material is clumpy. That affects the precise ratios. The detection of the rare molecule is the central result; a complete explanation of how much of it formed, and through which reactions, remains open.

## What this does and does not tell us

The observation shows that interstellar chemistry can produce an unusually heavy form of a familiar organic molecule near a forming star. It does not establish that this molecule has reached a planet, or that the region contains life. Instead, it gives laboratory chemists and modelers a demanding new measurement to explain.

As COMPASS compares other young stars, researchers can ask whether this isotope pattern is common or depends on a cloud's temperature, age, or history. That is one way to follow the chemical ingredients of future planetary systems back toward the cold clouds where their stars began.
